title: How A Simple, First-Week-Of-School Classroom Procedure Can Inspire Excellence In Your Students
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Using lining up as a case study, Linsin argues that teaching everyday classroom procedures with rigor instills habits of excellence that carry over into academic work. He opens with a Colin Powell quote about habits of excellence and contends that a sloppy line predicts sloppy academic behavior. The article lays out a five-step teaching method: model the procedure yourself, have one student practice it, model with a small group, have groups practice independently, and finally have the whole class perform it under observation, repeating until it is done correctly. He recommends revisiting the procedure the next day with a short refresher and re-teaching it anytime standards slip during the year, even if it costs students time at recess. The piece closes by connecting procedural simplicity and clarity to broader academic excellence, arguing that clear expectations, not watered-down content, are what let learning flourish.
points: Teach routine procedures like lining up during the first few days of school, since they're simple, frequent, and set a pattern for everything else.
Follow a five-step teaching sequence: model it yourself, have one student model, model with a small group, let groups practice independently, then run it with the whole class.
Revisit the procedure with a short refresher the next day, and re-teach anytime performance slips, even if it costs the class time later.
Give students a scripted courtesy exchange (an extended arm and 'After you'/'Thank you') to build politeness directly into the routine.
Treat simplification, not simplification of curriculum, as the goal: clear, elemental instructions let excellence become habitual.
quotes: If you are going to achieve excellence in big things, you develop the habit in little matters. ~Colin Powell
In other words, by requiring excellence from your students for everyday procedures, like lining up to leave your classroom, you’re ingraining habits that make them better students.
If your line is noisy, pushy, and looks like Lombard Street, then you’ll struggle to manage your students during academic work as well.

Choose four or five students to line up with you, again on your signal. As you’re filing into a straight and comfortably spaced line, show them how to politely extend an arm and say, “After you,” as well as how to respond with a nod and a curt, “Thank you.
The initial lesson should only take ten minutes or so. But it’s a good idea to revisit the procedure the next day—a quick five-minute refresher should be sufficient.

When you break your lessons down to their most elemental parts, when you cut out the superfluous and make your instructions strikingly clear and doable, when you show your class exactly what you want and then let them practice and perfect their skills…
